candidates.attacker_control: The attacker controls the bearer access token (any valid, non-expired user token issued for the target realm, e.g. obtained by logging in as a normal account) and the {id} path parameter (a target user UUID). No realm-management role, no special client and no server-side configuration change by the victim is needed beyond organizations being enabled in the realm.
candidates.counterevidence_checked: I checked whether the endpoint is protected upstream: every sibling method in the same resource performs auth.realm().requireManageRealm() (create at line 90, search at line 138, get at line 155), so the omission is inconsistent with the surrounding access-control pattern. I traced the admin API front door to confirm it only authenticates the token and checks the realm (AdminRoot.java 164-194/210-230, RealmsAdminResource.java 194-209) and does not impose a realm-admin role. I verified the JAX-RS path is reachable directly (literal template members/{id}/organizations matches the full remaining path, so it is not shadowed by the guarded @Path("{id}") locator). I also confirmed the delegate OrganizationMemberResource.getOrganizations() contains no hidden check when the resource is constructed with organization == null. No runtime testing was performed.
candidates.impact: An authenticated but unprivileged user can read which organizations another user (or any known user id) belongs to, including organization metadata such as domains and attributes. In deployments that use organizations for tenant isolation, this discloses cross-tenant user-to-organization mappings and organization details through an interface that the same code base otherwise guards with requireManageRealm().
candidates.prerequisites: 1) ORGANIZATION feature enabled and at least one organization present in the realm (Organizations.checkEnabled is also skipped on this path, but an empty provider would only reduce the impact). 2) A valid access token for the realm, which any authenticated user of that realm possesses. 3) Knowledge of a target user's id (UUID) to enumerate that user's memberships; the caller can always use their own id, and ids obtainable elsewhere (e.g., from links/tokens) make other users enumerable.
candidates.root_cause: OrganizationsResource.getOrganizations(), which handles GET /admin/realms/{realm}/organizations/members/{id}/organizations directly, does not perform any permission check before delegating to OrganizationMemberResource.getOrganizations(id). Unlike the sibling methods create(), search() and get() in the same class, which all call auth.realm().requireManageRealm() (and Organizations.checkEnabled), this handler omits the check entirely, and the delegate OrganizationMemberResource.getOrganizations() has no access-control logic of its own (it only calls session.users().getUserById() and provider.getByMember()). The admin API entry points AdminRoot.getRealmsAdmin()/authenticateRealmAdminRequest() and RealmsAdminResource.getRealmAdmin() merely authenticate the bearer token and match the token realm (AdminRoot.java lines 164-194, 210-230; RealmsAdminResource.java lines 194-209); they do not require realm-management roles, so endpoint-level checks are the only authorization boundary.
candidates.title: Missing authorization check on admin organizations membership endpoint (OrganizationsResource.getOrganizations)
candidates.trace: HTTP GET /admin/realms/{realm}/organizations/members/{id}/organizations -> AdminRoot.getRealmsAdmin() (admin API enabled) -> authenticateRealmAdminRequest() validates the bearer token only -> RealmsAdminResource.getRealmAdmin() enforces only that the token realm matches the requested realm -> RealmAdminResource.organizations() -> OrganizationsResource.getOrganizations(id) (lines 179-181; no auth.realm().requireManageRealm() and no other check) -> OrganizationMemberResource.getOrganizations(id) (lines 192-200; no check) -> getUser(id) via session.users().getUserById() -> provider.getByMember(member) -> ModelToRepresentation.toRepresentation() streams org id/name/alias/enabled/redirectUrl/description/domains/attributes back to the caller.
candidates.unverified: No runtime/authz test was executed; reachability by a plain user token is inferred from the authentication code path (BearerTokenAuthenticator only checks token validity/realm) rather than observed. Whether the upstream intended fix used requireManageRealm() or a user-level permission (e.g. auth.users().requireView(user)) is unconfirmed; either way a check is absent. Sensitivity of returned user ids and organization attributes for a given deployment is deployment-dependent.
candidates.weakness_type: Missing Authorization (CWE-862) / Improper Authorization (CWE-863), information disclosure (CWE-200)

coverage_summary: The source scope is 5619 model-visible files (4495 Java) with no binary/sensitive-path exclusions. The P1 relation index is partial: 5564 files indexed, 55 source files missing from the index, 414 files parsed for symbols, 0 parse errors, and semantic resolution/control-flow/data-flow are explicitly not implemented, so index edges/facts were used only as navigation hints and every reported fact was re-verified in source text. I searched and/or read representative security-critical areas including the OIDC authorization/token/PKCE/redirect logic, SAML signature validation and XML parsing, admin REST authentication and permission evaluation, organizations (admin resources, login authenticator, OIDC mapper/scope), credential providers (password, OTP/TOTP, recovery codes, WebAuthn), LDAP escaping, theme/resource loading, HTTP client and CIBA configuration, OID4VC proof validation, and the JS UI shared library. Not every one of the ~5600 files was read line-by-line, so other issues may remain uninspected; the missing authorization check was selected as the single strongest, best-evidenced candidate.
limitations: Static source review only: no code was built, executed, or tested, and no runtime authorization behavior (e.g. acceptance of a plain user token by the admin API) was observed; the exploitability conclusion is inferred from the authentication/permission code.

The P1 relation index is partial and explicitly lacks semantic resolution, control flow and data flow; 55 source files are missing from it and call/containment edges are syntactic candidates only. Areas not represented in the index (and all non-Java artifacts such as .tsx files, which are absent from the snapshot) were not systematically reviewed.
Only one candidate could be submitted; several lower-confidence leads were rejected and are listed for completeness.

No comparison against upstream fixed code, patches, CVE/CWE ground truth, or sibling-condition outputs was performed, so whether this missing check corresponds to the case's intended issue is unconfirmed.

rejected_leads.lead: Organization membership claim taken from a user-supplied login form parameter: OrganizationAuthenticator.resolveOrganization() (services/src/main/java/org/keycloak/organization/authentication/authenticators/browser/OrganizationAuthenticator.java lines 132-154) sets the client note 'kc.org' from the kc.org request parameter without verifying organization.isMember(user); OrganizationMembershipMapper.setClaim() (services/src/main/java/org/keycloak/organization/protocol/mappers/oidc/OrganizationMembershipMapper.java lines 112-140) then emits the claim for that organization id without a membership check, unlike OrganizationScope (which filters by membership).
rejected_leads.reason: Plausible improper-authorization lead, but several conditions remain unverified in source-only review: whether the auth-session client note is guaranteed to propagate to the authenticated client session used by the mapper, whether the organization mapper is configured on affected clients, and whether relying parties treat the claim as authoritative. Reported only as an unconfirmed secondary lead; not strong enough to displace the concrete missing-check candidate.

rejected_leads.lead: WebAuthn authenticator counter update uses the stored counter instead of the newly received sign count: services/src/main/java/org/keycloak/credential/WebAuthnCredentialProvider.java lines 220-227 reads auth.getCount() (persisted value) and stores count+1 rather than authenticationData.getAuthenticatorData().getSignCount().
rejected_leads.reason: May weaken clone-detection semantics, but it is at most a hardening/robustness weakness (webauthn4j already validates the incoming counter against the stored value before this code runs), and the surrounding code/comment matches long-standing upstream behavior; it does not by itself enable authentication bypass.

rejected_leads.lead: Odd-looking but non-security-relevant artifacts noticed while sampling: testsuite InputServlet.doPost() prints a constant 'parameter=hello' instead of reflecting the posted parameter (testsuite/integration-arquillian/test-apps/servlets/src/main/java/org/keycloak/testsuite/adapter/servlet/InputServlet.java line 83); HmacOTP/HardcodedLDAPAttributeMapper secret alphabets omit XYZ (server-spi/src/main/java/org/keycloak/models/utils/HmacOTP.java line 48).
rejected_leads.reason: Both are in test-only or low-impact code (constant echo removes, not adds, reflection; missing alphabet characters only marginally reduce generated-secret entropy and appear consistently in two files, suggesting an upstream copy/paste quirk). Neither meets the evidence threshold for a candidate.

summary: Reviewed the Keycloak snapshot (5619 visible files; 4495 Java) as a defensive source review, using the P1 relation index for navigation and verifying each lead in source text. The strongest distinct issue found is a missing authorization check on an organization-membership admin endpoint: OrganizationsResource.getOrganizations() serves GET /admin/realms/{realm}/organizations/members/{id}/organizations and simply delegates to OrganizationMemberResource.getOrganizations(), which performs no permission check. Every other method in the same resource (create, search, get-organization) calls auth.realm().requireManageRealm(); the admin REST front door (AdminRoot.getRealmsAdmin / authenticateRealmAdminRequest) only authenticates the bearer token and checks that the token's realm matches, so endpoint-level authorization is the only control. As a result, any authenticated user holding a valid access token for the realm can enumerate the organizations a given user belongs to (id, name, alias, enabled flag, description, domains and attributes), a cross-tenant information disclosure. Secondary observations (organization-claim handling and WebAuthn counter update) are noted as unconfirmed rejected leads.
